strengths: Addresses an important and practical challenge in clinical AI: bridging the gap between static medical question-answering and dynamic, multi-turn clinical inquiry under uncertainty.

The two-tiered reward design incorporating a hierarchical safety veto mechanism is well-motivated for safety-critical healthcare settings, effectively penalizing catastrophic medical advice or unsound reasoning.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across diverse multi-turn dialogue benchmarks (HealthBench Main/Hard, MAQuE) and static QA (MedQA, MMLU), demonstrating competitive performance against substantially larger models and proprietary baselines.
Informative ablation and scaling studies analyzing the contributions of the experience retrieval module, interaction turn depth, and the volume of simulated patient training interactions.
weaknesses: Reliance on an 8B model (Qwen3-8B) as the Consultation Evaluator across 8 multi-faceted dimensions raises questions regarding reward consistency and evaluation fidelity. While prompt rubrics and CoT are used, the paper lacks quantitative validation (e.g., inter-rater reliability or agreement metrics against board-certified physicians) for the automated evaluator.

The human evaluation was conducted with only five annotators without clinical expertise. While suitable for judging bedside manner and empathy from a patient perspective, non-experts are ill-equipped to validate clinical accuracy, safety adherence, or diagnostic validity in complex cases.

The role of the experience repository at inference time needs clearer disentanglement. Prepending retrieved past experiences to the prompt acts as a form of few-shot / in-context retrieval augmentation; the paper should clarify how much performance gain is attributable to test-time retrieval versus the reinforced policy itself, along with the associated latency overhead during real-time multi-turn interaction.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem in clinical AI: bridging the gap between static medical QA benchmarks and dynamic, multi-turn clinical inquiry under uncertainty.

Well-structured framework combining multi-agent interactive simulation, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), a two-tiered reward function (dense conversational process reward with a hierarchical veto mechanism + sparse diagnostic outcome reward), and an experience repository.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple clinical benchmarks (HealthBench Main/Hard, MAQuE, MedQA, MMLU) demonstrating consistent improvements over competitive 7B-8B and larger open-source models, as well as proprietary baselines.
Thorough empirical analysis, including dialogue turn scaling, patient volume scaling, component ablations, and a detailed clinical case study.
weaknesses: The human evaluation was conducted exclusively with five non-expert annotators. While lay annotators can evaluate subjective communication aspects (e.g., perceived empathy or clarity), evaluating diagnostic reasoning, information gathering strategy, and clinical adherence fundamentally requires trained clinical professionals.

The training pipeline relies heavily on an LLM judge (Qwen3-8B) as the process reward model across eight complex dimensions. The paper does not provide quantitative validation (e.g., correlation or agreement rates with licensed physicians) to demonstrate that an 8B evaluator reliably scores nuanced medical safety and reasoning quality.

Algorithmic novelty is relatively incremental, as the methodology primarily integrates existing components: POMDP multi-agent rollouts, standard GRPO, heuristic multi-attribute prompt-based reward scoring, and embedding-plus-reranking retrieval for episodic memory.

There are minor inconsistencies and typos in the manuscript: Section A mentions that the reward model evaluates 'across five weighted dimensions, yielding a raw score in [-10, 10]', which contradicts Section 3.2 and Appendix A.1 describing eight dimensions scored on [-5, 5]; Figure 1 caption has 'Medical Desion Task'; page 4 contains 'polify of the doctor agent'; and page 25 has 'Wwe implemented'.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely clinical problem: bridging the gap between static biomedical knowledge retrieval and dynamic, multi-turn diagnostic consultation under uncertainty.
The proposed framework incorporates an intuitive set of components, combining multi-agent patient simulation, a hierarchical safety-veto reward structure, and experiential retrieval.
The experimental evaluation covers diverse benchmarks (HealthBench Main and Hard, MAQuE, MedQA, MMLU) as well as scaling analyses over dialogue turns and patient agent counts.
The appendix provides extensive implementation details, including complete system prompts, hyperparameter specifications, and an illustrative clinical case study.
weaknesses: Fundamental flaw in theoretical formulation: Equation (1) claims to specify the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) objective, but instead presents a Plackett-Luce / listwise ranking loss solely over reward model outputs $R_\psi$, completely omitting the policy parameters $\theta$ and the token probability ratios characteristic of policy gradient / GRPO methods.

Lack of professional clinical validation: The human evaluation exclusively utilizes five lay annotators without medical training. While acceptable for perceived clarity and empathy, this leaves clinical accuracy, differential diagnosis rigor, and safety completely unverified by medical experts.

Unverified reward model fidelity: The training process relies on an 8B LLM judge to provide dense process rewards across complex medical axes (e.g., medical accuracy, reasoning soundness, safety). The paper does not provide quantitative calibration or agreement studies (e.g., Cohen's kappa against board-certified physicians) to validate the medical reliability of this 8B critic.

Methodological shortcuts on static benchmarks: Factual retention evaluations on MedQA and MMLU were run only on arbitrarily sampled subsets of 200 questions without standard errors or multiple trials, rather than using the standard, full benchmark test splits, making the dramatic reported gain (+20% on MedQA) unconvincing.

Theoretical and algorithmic ambiguity in experiential RL: Injecting dynamically retrieved historical trajectories into the doctor agent prompt alters the effective state space during policy optimization, yet the paper lacks theoretical grounding or discussion on how this non-stationarity impacts on-policy training stability and credit assignment.

Internal contradictions and writing errors: Section 3.2 and Table 4 detail an 8-dimensional process reward, whereas Appendix A mentions scoring across 'five weighted dimensions'. Furthermore, there are multiple typos and formatting glitches (e.g., 'Static Medical Desion Task' in Figure 1, 'polify' on page 4, 'Wwe' on page 25, and corrupted text box artifacts in Figure 2).

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem in clinical AI: bridging the gap between static QA knowledge and dynamic, multi-turn clinical inquiry under uncertainty.

Well-designed technical architecture integrating multi-agent environment simulation, a two-tiered reward scheme with a safety/accuracy veto mechanism, and an experiential retrieval pipeline optimized via GRPO.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning standard dynamic clinical benchmarks (HealthBench Main and Hard, MAQuE), static QA benchmarks (MedQA, MMLU), and dual-cohort human evaluations (layperson patient experience and licensed physician assessment).

Extensive ablation studies that thoroughly isolate individual components, including comparisons among GRPO, PPO, and SFT, verification of experience retrieval modules (state vs. action, novelty/reward filtering), safety veto ablation, and transferability across model families (Qwen and Llama).
Detailed qualitative analysis and failure mode examination in the appendix, offering transparency into how the agent handles high-stakes scenarios and where omissions occur.
weaknesses: The process reward and consultation evaluator rely heavily on an 8B LLM judge (Qwen3-8B). As shown in the cross-evaluator study (Table 14 and Section E.3), the correlation between the 8B judge and human physicians is relatively modest (Spearman's rank correlation around 0.24), indicating non-negligible evaluator noise.

Because the experience module retrieves prior trajectory information into the prompt during inference, part of the performance gain is attributable to test-time context augmentation (similar to in-context episodic retrieval/RAG), which slightly blurs how much policy improvement comes purely from reinforcement learning versus prompt conditioning.

The evaluation setup includes model references (such as GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4, Grok-4) whose exact versions, availability, and access conditions should be clearly documented to ensure external reproducibility.

strengths: Addresses a crucial and timely challenge in medical AI: transitioning from static medical QA to dynamic, strategic, and empathetic multi-turn clinical inquiry under uncertainty.

Comprehensive and principled system design: effectively integrates a multi-agent POMDP formulation, an 8-dimensional two-tiered process/outcome reward scheme with a safety veto mechanism, and an experiential retrieval module combining semantic similarity, reward weighting, and novelty filtering.
Extensive and rigorous experimental evaluation spanning multiple challenging benchmarks (HealthBench Main/Hard, MAQuE, MedQA, MMLU) across both open-source and proprietary models.

Thorough human evaluations conducted with both licensed medical experts (clinical validity, utility of retrieved experiences) and patient-perspective annotators (empathy, clarity, coherence), supported by inter-rater correlation analysis.

High-quality ablations and analyses, including comparisons between GRPO, PPO, and SFT, transferability to alternative model backbones (Llama-3.1-8B), component isolating studies for retrieved experiences, scaling trends with simulated patient volume, and computational overhead profiling.
weaknesses: Simulation-to-reality gap: The training environment relies heavily on LLM-simulated patient personas. While proactive prompting and post-filtering (13.82% rejection rate) mitigate out-of-character behaviors, synthetic interactions may not fully capture the nuance, unpredictability, and miscommunication patterns of real-world clinical consultations.

Reliance on LLM-as-a-Judge for reward modeling: The Consultation Evaluator is instantiated with an 8B model (Qwen3-8B). Although rubrics and CoT prompting are applied, automated evaluation of subtle medical reasoning and safety nuances remains prone to occasional misjudgments or reward exploitation.

Unconventional or speculative model versions referenced in the baseline tables (e.g., GPT-5, Grok-4, Claude Sonnet 4, Qwen3) without full documentation on access configurations, which slightly clouds reproducibility and standardization against published academic baselines.

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation: Addresses the critical gap between static medical QA benchmarks and dynamic, interactive clinical inquiry where adaptive questioning, safety triage, and bedside empathy are required.

Comprehensive and coherent framework: The integration of multi-agent POMDP formulation, two-tiered reward architecture with hierarchical safety vetoes, GRPO optimization, and a reward/novelty-filtered experience repository is well-designed and technically sound.

Strong empirical results: The proposed 8B model achieves competitive or superior performance compared to larger open-source medical models (e.g., Baichuan-M2-32B, UltraMedical-70B) and frontier proprietary models across both HealthBench (Main & Hard) and MAQuE benchmarks.

Extensive ablation and analysis: Thorough ablations covering RL algorithms (SFT vs. PPO vs. GRPO), experience retrieval components (state vs. action, novelty/reward filtering), reward structure (veto system, soft-skill weights), architecture transferability (Llama-3.1-8B), training scaling laws, and computational overhead.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on LLM-based reward modeling: The dense process reward depends on a Qwen3-8B evaluator rating eight fine-grained dimensions and executing hierarchical vetoes. Despite mitigation efforts, automated LLM reward signals in clinical domains remain prone to hallucination, bias, and subtle reward hacking.

Modest human expert correlation and limited expert cohort: The validation with licensed physicians involves only two physicians on a relatively small sample (40–80 cases). Furthermore, the Spearman rank correlation between the Qwen3-8B evaluator and human experts is reported as low-to-moderate (rho > 0.24), which undermines the claim of high agreement with expert judgment.

Potential risk of train-test overlap: The training pipeline utilizes 100k synthetic dialogues generated with LLM assistance. A clearer analysis of scenario overlap or contamination between the training patient scenarios and the evaluation benchmark cases (HealthBench and MAQuE) is needed.

Minor presentation and reporting issues: Several typos and overstated claims exist (e.g., describing a Spearman rho of 0.24 as 'moderate high'; missing words in Section 1 'substantial improvement in with an increase of +9.91').
